creator: Alexander Terp
description:
RESOLVED 2026-08-10 via option 2. `split()` and `replace()` now match literally, with a `regex: bool = false` parameter to opt into pattern matching. `matches()` is unchanged and stays regex-always, since a literal `matches()` would be `==` or a substring test.

The sibling of this card - "Add escape_regex()", option 3 - was repurposed into that work. See sprint card `literal-string-defaults`.

Every symptom listed below is gone:

- `"a.b.c".replace(".", "-")` -> `"a-b-c"`
- `"a.b.c".split(".")` -> `["a", "b", "c"]`
- `"a(b".split("(")` -> `["a", "b"]`, no RAD20024 and no silent literal fallback
- `replace()`'s replacement string is literal by default, so `$0` and `$1` in relayed text pass through untouched

Migration is carried by RAD40016, a checker warning that flags literal patterns reading as regexes with no `regex=`, plus `docs-web/docs/migrations/v0.12.md`.

---

Original report, re-verified 2026-06-14 (rad v0.10.1):

**The problem:**
- `"a.b.c".replace(".", "-")` -> "-----"  (`.` is regex "any char")
- `"a.b.c".split(".")` -> ["", "", "", "", "", ""]
- Regex metacharacters like `(` raise error[RAD20024] "Error compiling regex pattern"
- The replacement arg also uses regex semantics ($0, capture groups)

**Source:** `core/func_replace.go:20`, `core/func_split.go:32` - both `regexp.Compile` user input.

**Why it matters:** most users expect literal string ops by default; docs show `text.replace("hello", "hi")` which looks literal. Users must hand-escape regex metacharacters.

**Possible solutions:**
1. Add `replace_literal()` / `split_literal()`
2. Make replace/split literal by default, add `replace_regex()` / `split_regex()`
3. Add an `escape_regex()` utility
title: replace() and split() treat first arg as regex, not literal string
